FHSA qualifying withdrawal: map the purchase dates and the account-closing clock

Lay a hypothetical home purchase on a calendar to see how the FHSA qualifying-withdrawal checkpoints, the 1 October acquisition deadline and the shortened participation period fit together, and what happens to money left in the account.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Original hypothetical calendar, not tax advice. It applies a simplified version of the CRA conditions reviewed 26 October 2026: acquisition no more than 30 days before the withdrawal; acquisition or construction completion before 1 October of the year after the withdrawal; occupancy, or intent to occupy, within one year after acquisition; and no owner-occupied principal residence in the previous four calendar years. It does not test the current-year part of the look-back, the written-agreement requirement, Form RC725, continuous Canadian residence, construction specifics, survivor or successor-holder rules, issuer processing time or any HBP condition. The participation period ends 31 December of the earliest trigger year. The tax rate is an editable illustration; withholding, credits and province are not calculated, and the balance is held flat. Dates: withdrawal 2027-03-15, acquisition 2027-04-29, occupancy 2027-05-29.

The central idea

A qualifying FHSA withdrawal is tested against dated checkpoints, and the first one also starts a short closing clock: the account must be emptied or transferred by 31 December of the following year, or the leftover value is taxed.

01

Two calendars run at once

The contribution side of a First Home Savings Account (FHSA) is annual: participation room, carry-forward and deductions are counted by calendar year. The withdrawal side runs on dates. When you take money out to buy a home, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) tests that withdrawal against the date you acquire the home, the following 1 October, and when you move in. The same first qualifying withdrawal also moves forward the date by which every FHSA you hold must be closed.

The explorer models one hypothetical buyer. They open their first FHSA in 2024, reach age 30 that year and have never lived in a home they owned. On 15 March 2027 they withdraw CAD 30,000 of a CAD 33,500 balance as a qualifying withdrawal. The purchase closes 45 days later, on 29 April 2027, and they move in one month after that. Every figure below is original arithmetic on those invented dates; none of it describes a real person or account.

02

The dated checkpoints for a qualifying withdrawal

CRA’s withdrawals page (modified 10 February 2026) lists the conditions that must be met at the time of a qualifying withdrawal. In plain terms, you must be a resident of Canada; you must have a written agreement to buy or build a qualifying home with an acquisition or construction-completion date before 1 October of the year after the withdrawal; you must not have acquired the home more than 30 days before the withdrawal; you must intend to occupy it as your principal residence within one year after acquiring it; and you must meet the first-time home buyer test that applies to withdrawals. You make the request to your issuer using Form RC725. Residency must continue from the first qualifying withdrawal until the earlier of acquiring the home or death.

The first-time home buyer test for withdrawals is not the same as the one for opening an account. For a withdrawal, you must not have lived in a home that you, alone or jointly, owned as your principal residence at any time in the current calendar year before the withdrawal (other than the 30 days immediately before it) or in any of the four preceding calendar years. In the default case the buyer has never owned a home, so the look-back is passed. The explorer’s simplified look-back only checks whether the last owner-occupied year is at least five years before the withdrawal year. Enter 2023 with a 2027 withdrawal to see it fail.

The first chart turns each checkpoint into days of margin. The 30-day rule leaves 75 days, because the home is acquired 45 days after the withdrawal rather than up to 30 days before it. The acquisition deadline leaves 520 days between 29 April 2027 and the last permitted day, 30 September 2028. Occupancy one month after acquisition leaves 336 days before the one-year mark of 29 April 2028. If any bar is negative, the withdrawal in this model would not be qualifying. CRA says it would then be a taxable withdrawal that must be included in income for the year received, reassessing an already-assessed return if necessary. CRA also states that a qualifying withdrawal cannot be cancelled once made.

03

The first qualifying withdrawal shortens the account’s life

CRA’s closing page (modified 2 February 2026) says the maximum participation period begins when you open your first FHSA and ends on 31 December of the year in which the earliest of three events occurs: the 15th anniversary of opening your first FHSA, the year you turn 71, or the year following your first qualifying withdrawal. For the default buyer those years are 2039, 2065 and 2028, so the account’s period ends on 31 December 2028, 657 days after the 15 March 2027 withdrawal.

The fourth chart repeats the calculation for first-withdrawal years from 2024 onward. A withdrawal in any year from opening up to 2038 makes the following year the binding trigger. With no qualifying withdrawal, the 15th anniversary in 2039 binds for this buyer. Someone who opens an account at an older age can find the age-71 trigger binding instead: set the opening age to 60 and the period ends in 2035 without a withdrawal. Later qualifying withdrawals for the same purchase are possible while the account remains open and the conditions are met, but they do not restart the clock.

CRA’s published examples follow this rule. One example on the closing page refers to both 2031 and 2032 for the same first qualifying withdrawal; the guide relies on the rule text rather than that example.

04

What to do with any amount left in the account

A buyer does not have to withdraw the whole balance. In the default case CAD 3,500 is left after the CAD 30,000 qualifying withdrawal. CRA describes three outcomes for property still in an FHSA as the period approaches its end. You can generally transfer it directly to your RRSP or RRIF on a tax-deferred basis; the withdrawals page adds that such a direct transfer does not affect unused RRSP deduction room, whereas withdrawing cash and re-contributing it would. You can make a taxable withdrawal, which is income for the year you receive it and is reported in box 22 of the T4FHSA slip, with income tax withheld at source. If property remains after the period ends, the accounts stop being FHSAs and the fair market value at the end of 31 December is included in income, reported in box 26 of the T4FHSA. CRA recommends closing all FHSAs before the period ends.

The third chart uses an editable 30% marginal rate to show the stakes. A direct transfer keeps the full CAD 3,500 inside a registered plan. A taxable withdrawal or deemed income at the same rate would cost about CAD 1,050 in tax, leaving CAD 2,450. The final row shows the larger risk: if the CAD 30,000 withdrawal later turned out not to be qualifying — for example because the purchase fell through and no home was acquired before the deadline — the full amount would be taxable, about CAD 9,000 at the illustrative rate. That rate is a placeholder, not a statutory rate or a forecast of anyone’s tax; actual tax depends on province, other income, credits and the year.

05

Stress-test the dates before signing

Use the explorer to try the situations that commonly squeeze the calendar. Set the acquisition lag to −31 to see the 30-day rule fail when a buyer takes possession first and withdraws too late. Move the withdrawal to December and lengthen the lag for a new-build whose completion date slips: a withdrawal on 15 December 2027 leaves the purchase until 30 September 2028, under ten months. Push occupancy beyond 12 months to see the intention test fail. Lower the qualifying amount to see how much would have to be transferred to an RRSP or RRIF before the closing deadline.

The model leaves out several conditions on purpose because they cannot be reduced to a date: the written agreement and its terms, what counts as a qualifying home, continuous Canadian residence, construction contracts, disability-related home rules in other programmes, survivor and successor-holder treatment, and your issuer’s own processing time. It also holds the balance flat and does not compute withholding. Using the RRSP Home Buyers’ Plan for the same home is allowed if each programme’s conditions are met at the time of each withdrawal, but the plan’s separate repayment schedule is covered in the related guide, not here.

Before requesting a withdrawal, confirm the current CRA conditions, ask the issuer how long Form RC725 processing takes, keep the purchase agreement and closing documents, and diary the 31 December closing date for any remainder. A qualified tax professional can check the parts this calendar does not.
